etymology: Hebrew beth-’arbel, “house of God’s ambush” or “house of the lying in wait,” a town remembered by the prophet Hosea for a day of grievous battle.
biblical_def: Beth-arbel is named but once in the Scripture, and that in a word of warning. The prophet Hosea, foretelling the ruin that would come upon the northern kingdom for her idolatry, sets before the people a remembered slaughter: as Shalman spoiled Beth-arbel in the day of battle, when the mother was dashed in pieces upon her children (Hos 10:14). The town and the day are alike obscure to us; the lesson is not. The prophet calls a known horror to mind that Israel might tremble at the horror coming upon herself, who had trusted in her own way and in the multitude of her mighty men. The dictionary does not labour to fix the place upon a map; it honours rather what the LORD honours, that even a forgotten field of blood is set in His word as a witness to the wages of forsaking Him. He who measured out the goodly heritage of His people also numbered the days of their chastisement when they spurned His covenant. Beth-arbel stands therefore as a sober marker upon the sacred geography: a name spoken once, in the day of battle, to teach that the bounds of habitation and the bounds of judgment are alike in the hand of God, and that no people is so settled in their portion that they may sin and not be visited.

etymology: Hebrew beth-ba’al-me’on, “house of the lord of the dwelling,” a town of the tribe of Reuben upon the high plain east of the Jordan.
biblical_def: Beth-baal-meon was a town in the upland country east of the Jordan, reckoned to the tribe of Reuben when Moses and Joshua portioned out the land that had belonged to Sihon king of the Amorites. It is set among the cities of the plain, named with Heshbon and the towns thereof, in the inheritance of the children of Reuben (Jos 13:17). The name carries the memory of the false worship of the land, for Baal-meon means the dwelling of Baal; yet the LORD took this very place from the hand of the heathen and gave it to His own people for a possession, that where idols had been served the name of the true God might be confessed. The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of the place; what it honours is that the LORD numbered even this border town of Reuben among the goodly heritage He measured out east of the river. The lines were fallen unto Reuben in pleasant places, and the bounds of his habitation were not the work of chance or of the sword alone, but of the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Beth-baal-meon stands as a witness that the LORD is able to take the very houses of false gods and set His people to dwell in them, turning the strongholds of idolatry into the heritage of the saints.

etymology: Hebrew beth-ha’emeq, “house of the valley,” a town upon the border of the tribe of Asher in the north of the land.
biblical_def: Beth-emek was a town that marked the border of the tribe of Asher when Joshua divided the inheritance among the children of Israel by lot in Shiloh. It is named in the tracing of Asher’s boundary, which turned toward the rising of the sun to Beth-dagon and reached to Zebulun and to the valley of Jiphthah-el, to Beth-emek and Neiel, going out on the left hand to Cabul (Jos 19:27). The name itself, the house of the valley, marks its situation in the low country of the north, among the pleasant places of Asher near the sea. The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of its geography; what it honours is that the LORD numbered even this little border town among the goodly heritage He measured out to His people. Asher was promised that his bread should be fat and that he should yield royal dainties, and that his shoes should be iron and brass (Gen 49:20; Deu 33:24-25); and the LORD made good His word in the very stones of the boundary. The lines were fallen unto Asher in pleasant places, and the bounds of his habitation were not the work of chance, but of the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Beth-emek stands as a witness that no border of the saint’s heritage is too small for the care of Him who apportioned it.

etymology: Hebrew beth-ha’etsel, “house of the side” or “house of the neighbour,” a town of the low country named by the prophet Micah in his lament over the cities of Judah.
biblical_def: Beth-ezel is named once, in the prophet Micah’s mournful roll-call of the towns of the Shephelah that would feel the rod of judgment when the Assyrian came up against the land. Micah, with a holy play upon the names of the places, declares that the inhabitant of Saphir should pass away in shame, that the inhabitant of Zaanan came not forth, and that the mourning of Beth-ezel should take from the people its standing-place (Mic 1:11). The town lay among the cities of the southern low country, near to Lachish and the border towns of Judah. The dictionary does not labour to fix it upon a map; what it honours is that the LORD set even this small town within the inheritance of His people, and named it in His word as a witness to His righteous dealing. He who measured out the goodly heritage of Judah also numbered the day of her chastisement when she trusted in her strong cities rather than in her God. The lines had fallen unto Judah in pleasant places, yet the same God who gave the land would visit the iniquity of those who dwelt in it. Beth-ezel stands therefore upon the sacred geography as a sober marker, the house of the neighbour that could lend no help in the day of trouble, teaching that no city of refuge avails the soul that forsakes the LORD, and that the bounds of habitation and the bounds of judgment are alike in His hand.

etymology: Hebrew beth-gader, “house of the wall” or “house of the hedge,” a town of Judah named in the genealogies of the first book of Chronicles.
biblical_def: Beth-gader appears in the genealogies of Judah recorded by the chronicler, where the families of the descendants of Caleb and of Hur are set down with the towns they founded or fathered. Hareph is named as the father of Beth-gader, even as other men of Judah are named as fathers of Kirjath-jearim, of Beth-lehem, and of other towns of the inheritance (1Ch 2:51). In the manner of the Hebrew, to be the father of a town is to be its founder or chief, the head of the men who built and dwelt there. The town lay in the hill country of Judah, and its name, the house of the wall, marks it as a place fenced and settled in the goodly heritage. The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of its situation; what it honours is that the LORD wrote even these small towns and their founders into His word, that the generations of His people might be numbered and remembered. He who measured out the inheritance of Judah by lot also kept the record of the families that filled it. The lines were fallen unto Judah in pleasant places, and the bounds of their habitation were not the work of chance, but of the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). etymology: Hebrew beth-gamul, “house of the weaned” or “house of recompence,” a city of the plain country of Moab named in the prophecy of Jeremiah.
biblical_def: Beth-gamul was a city of Moab upon the high plain east of the Jordan, named in the long burden that the prophet Jeremiah pronounced against that proud and settled nation. In the roll of the cities upon which judgment was to fall, the prophet declares that it was come upon Holon, and upon Jahazah, and upon Mephaath, and upon Dibon, and upon Nebo, and upon Beth-gamul, and upon Beth-meon (Jer 48:23-24). Moab had been at ease from his youth, settled upon his lees, and had not been emptied from vessel to vessel; therefore his taste remained in him, and the LORD purposed to send him wanderers that should cause him to wander. The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of the place; what it honours is that the LORD named even this city of a heathen people in His word, for the bounds of the nations are in His hand no less than the borders of Israel. He who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people also appoints the day of their visitation when their pride is full (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Beth-gamul stands therefore upon the sacred geography as a witness that the God of Israel is the God of all the earth, who has determined the times before appointed and the bounds of every habitation, and who will recompense the proud, even in the house whose name is recompence.

etymology: Hebrew beth-hakkerem, “house of the vineyard,” a town of Judah used as a beacon-station and named again among the districts that repaired the wall of Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Beth-haccherem, the house of the vineyard, was a town of Judah set upon a height fit for a beacon, and it is named in two seasons of the people’s history. The prophet Jeremiah, calling the children of Benjamin to gather themselves to flee out of the midst of Jerusalem before the coming evil, bids them blow the trumpet in Tekoa and set up a sign of fire in Beth-haccherem, for evil appeareth out of the north and great destruction (Jer 6:1). In the days of the return, when the wall of Jerusalem was built again, Malchiah the son of Rechab, the ruler of part of Beth-haccherem, repaired the dung gate and set up its doors (Neh 3:14). The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of its situation; what it honours is that the LORD set even this little hill town within the inheritance of His people, fit to bear the warning fire in the day of trouble and to lend its rulers to the rebuilding of His city. The lines were fallen unto Judah in pleasant places, and the bounds of their habitation were the gift of the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Beth-haccherem stands as a witness that the LORD numbers every town of His heritage, and uses even the least to give warning and to build His walls again.

etymology: Hebrew beth-haran, a fenced town of the tribe of Gad upon the plain east of the Jordan, called also Beth-aram.
biblical_def: Beth-haran was a fenced city in the valley of the Jordan, built by the children of Gad when they received their inheritance east of the river. When the tribes of Reuben and Gad sought the land of Jazer and Gilead for their much cattle, Moses gave them the kingdom of Sihon and of Og; and the children of Gad built Dibon, and Ataroth, and Aroer, and Beth-nimrah, and Beth-haran, fenced cities, and folds for their sheep (Num 32:36). In the apportioning recorded by Joshua, the same town is named with Beth-nimrah and Succoth and Zaphon among the cities of the valley given to Gad, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon (Jos 13:27). The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of its situation; what it honours is that the LORD numbered even this border town among the goodly heritage He measured out east of the river. The lines were fallen unto Gad in pleasant places, and the bounds of their habitation were not the work of chance or of the sword alone, but of the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Beth-haran stands as a witness that no fenced city of the saint’s heritage, however small, is too little for the care of Him who apportioned it and made good every word of His promise.

etymology: Hebrew beth-choglah, “house of the partridge,” a town upon the border between Judah and Benjamin near the Jordan and the salt sea.
biblical_def: Beth-hoglah was a town near the lower Jordan and the salt sea, set upon the border that divided the inheritance of Judah from that of Benjamin when Joshua portioned out the land. In the tracing of Judah’s north border, the line went up toward Beth-hoglah and passed along by the north of Beth-arabah (Jos 15:6); and in the lot of the children of Benjamin, the border came down to Beth-hoglah and went out at the north bay of the salt sea, and the town is reckoned among the cities of Benjamin (Jos 18:19,21). Thus the little town stood upon the very seam of two inheritances, a witness to the exactness with which the LORD measured out the portion of each tribe. The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of its situation; what it honours is that the LORD set even this border town among the goodly heritage He divided to His people, that the bounds of every tribe might be sure. The lines were fallen unto Judah and to Benjamin in pleasant places, and the bounds of their habitation were not the work of chance, but of the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Beth-hoglah stands as a witness that He who removes not the ancient landmark Himself sets every border of the saint’s heritage with His own hand.

etymology: Hebrew beth-rechob, “house of the broad place” or “house of the street,” a town and region in the far north of the land, near Dan, afterward an Aramean stronghold.
biblical_def: Beth-rehob was a town and the region about it in the far north of the land, near the city of Laish that the Danites took and called Dan. When the children of Dan smote Laish and burned it with fire, the Scripture notes that the city was in the valley that lieth by Beth-rehob, far from the Zidonians, having no business with any man (Jdg 18:28). In the days of David the place is named among the Aramean powers, for when the children of Ammon hired the Syrians to fight against Israel, they took into their pay the Syrians of Beth-rehob and the Syrians of Zoba (2Sa 10:6). Thus Beth-rehob lay upon the very edge of the inheritance, where the borders of Israel met the lands of the heathen. The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of its situation; what it honours is that the LORD set the bounds of His people even unto this far northern valley, and ruled the heathen powers that bordered them. He who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people governs alike the portion of Israel and the strongholds of Aram (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Beth-rehob stands as a witness that no border of the saint’s heritage lies beyond the rule of God, and that the LORD who appointed the lot of Dan also held in His hand the hired armies of the north.
